title: EU AI Office opens its first high-risk audit wave as enforcement finally arrives
subtitle: Brussels and 24 national regulators — including France's CNIL, Germany's BfDI and Spain's AESIA — start technical-file audits under Article 11, targeting resume screening, credit scoring, and other Annex III systems.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: The European AI Office in Brussels this month begins its first scheduled wave of compliance inspections under the AI Act, working alongside 24 national market-surveillance authorities. France's CNIL, Germany's BfDI and Spain's AESIA are running the opening round, focused on Article 11 technical files for high-risk systems deployed after August 2. Initial requests target three regulated sectors: automated resume-screening tools used in HR, algorithmic credit-assessment systems in retail banking, and other Annex III use cases. September is the point at which global AI regulation shifts from preliminary administrative work to active statutory enforcement — after months of guidance documents and voluntary codes, providers now have to answer technical questions from named regulators.

The mechanics are worth understanding because Article 11 is not a light-touch review. It obliges providers of high-risk systems to maintain a technical file that documents the intended purpose, the risk-management system, data governance, the training and validation methodology, human oversight measures, and the accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity of the system. The audit is a paper exercise in the sense that regulators start with the file, but the file has to be true — audit teams can and will ask for reproducible evidence, source data samples, and the model artifacts referenced. A vendor whose file describes a training pipeline that no longer matches production is exposed.

This lands in a transatlantic split that the G20 Innovation Ministerial in Chapel Hill made explicit last week: the United States pushed and got endorsement for the "Carolina Principles," a lighter-touch framework that discourages new AI regulators, while Europe is doing the opposite in real time. The commercial consequence is that any product sold into both markets now sits on two operating models. Even providers that are not headquartered in the EU are captured if their systems produce output used in the EU — which for cloud-hosted AI products is effectively everyone. The high-risk audits that begin this month will produce the first public data on how the AI Act actually bites.

For a learner or an early-career engineer, the useful move is to read the AI Act's Article 11 and Annex IV once, on the record. They are the checklist that any AI product touching the EU has to be built against, and understanding them is a portable skill: the same categories — intended purpose, data lineage, human oversight, robustness, monitoring — are becoming the shape of AI compliance almost everywhere. Vendors that architected for Article 11 up front are the ones that will survive the next twelve months of audits without a rewrite.
